title: Data Integrity
overview: Data integrity means data are accurate and up to date, and it is most at risk when data are entered or transmitted. Paper 1 asks you to explain how validation and verification protect integrity, describe and apply the validation checks (range, format, length, presence, existence, limit, check digit), and describe and carry out verification during data entry (visual check, double entry) and data transfer (parity checks, parity block checks and checksums). A classic trap is claiming that validation proves data are correct.
syllabusPoints: Describe how data validation and data verification help protect the integrity of data.
Describe and use methods of data validation, including range check, format check, length check, presence check, existence check, limit check and check digit.
Describe and use methods of data verification during data entry, including visual check and double entry.
Describe and use methods of data verification during data transfer, including parity check (byte and block) and checksum.

definitions.definition: The requirement for data to be accurate, complete and up to date.
An automatic check by the computer that data entered are reasonable and meet set rules; it does not prove the data are correct.
Checking that data have been entered or transferred exactly as intended, i.e. the copy matches the original.
An extra digit calculated from the other digits of a code and added to it, so that errors in entering or reading the code can be detected.
An extra bit added to a byte so that the total number of 1s is even (even parity) or odd (odd parity), as agreed by sender and receiver.
Parity applied to each byte and to each bit position (column) across a block of bytes, so a single-bit error can be located and corrected.
A value calculated from a block of transmitted data (e.g. the sum of its bytes) and sent with it; the receiver recalculates it to detect errors.

sections.title: How validation and verification protect integrity
content: Errors most often enter a system when data are typed in or when they are sent from one device to another. Validation checks that input data are sensible and follow the rules set for that field, rejecting data that are the wrong type, in the wrong format or out of range. Verification checks that the data entered or received are the same as the original data. Used together, they greatly reduce errors, but neither can guarantee the data are true: a valid date of birth can still be the wrong person's date of birth, and a correctly verified copy of a wrong value is still wrong.
bullets: Validation = is it reasonable? (performed by the computer against rules).
Verification = is it the same as the original? (checked on entry or on transfer).
Several validation checks can be applied to one field, e.g. a password may have presence, length and format checks.

sections.title: Validation checks
content: A range check ensures a value lies between a lower and an upper bound, such as a percentage between 0 and 100. A limit check tests only one boundary, such as an age of no more than 120. A format check ensures data follow a set pattern, such as a date in DD/MM/YYYY form or a student ID of two letters followed by four digits. A length check ensures the number of characters is exactly, at least or at most a given number, such as a password of at least 8 characters. A presence check ensures a required field has not been left blank. An existence check ensures the value entered refers to something that actually exists, such as a customer ID in the customer file or a file name on disk. A type check ensures the data are of the expected data type, such as a whole number for a quantity.
bullets: Range vs limit: range has two boundaries, limit has one.
Format checks the pattern of characters; length checks only how many there are.
Validation is carried out by software as the data are entered, before they are stored or processed.

examples.label: Choosing checks for a booking form
examples.content:
Number of guests (1 to 8) → range check and type check (integer)
Email address → presence check and format check (contains @ and a domain)
Membership number → existence check (must be in the members file) and length check (exactly 6 characters)
Arrival date → format check (DD/MM/YYYY)

sections.title: Check digits
content: A check digit is calculated from the other digits of an identification number, such as an ISBN or a product barcode, and added to the end. When the number is entered or scanned, the same calculation is repeated; if the result does not match the check digit, an error is reported. One common method is modulo 11: multiply each digit by a weight, add the products, divide by 11 and use the remainder to produce the check digit (a remainder that would give 10 is written as X). Check digits detect most single-digit errors and transpositions, where two digits are swapped.
bullets: A check digit is a validation check on the number itself; it is part of the stored code.
It detects incorrect digits, transposed digits, and extra or missing digits.
Do not confuse a check digit (part of a stored code) with a checksum (sent with a block of transmitted data).

examples.label: Calculating and using a modulo-11 check digit
examples.content:
Code: 3 7 2 6, weights 5 4 3 2
Sum = 3×5 + 7×4 + 2×3 + 6×2 = 15 + 28 + 6 + 12 = 61
61 ÷ 11 = 5 remainder 6
Check digit = 11 − 6 = 5 → full code 37265

Checking on entry (weights 5 4 3 2 1): 61 + 5×1 = 66, and 66 ÷ 11 has remainder 0 → valid
If 73265 is typed by mistake: 35 + 12 + 6 + 12 + 5 = 70, remainder 4 → error detected

sections.title: Verification during data entry
content: In a visual check, the user reads through the data on screen and compares it with the original source document before confirming it. In double entry, the data are entered twice, often by different people or, for a new password, twice by the same person; the computer compares the two versions and only accepts the data if they match. Both reduce copying mistakes, but neither guarantees correctness: a visual check depends on the person noticing the error, and in double entry the same mistake could be made twice.
bullets: Visual check: cheap and quick, but unreliable for long or repetitive data.
Double entry: catches most typing errors, but takes twice as long to enter the data.
Neither method checks whether the source document itself is correct.

sections.title: Parity checks during data transfer
content: During transmission a bit can be flipped from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0 by interference. Before sending, the sender and receiver agree on even or odd parity. The sender counts the 1s in the seven data bits of each byte and sets the eighth (parity) bit so that the total number of 1s is even (or odd). The receiver counts the 1s in each byte it receives; if the count does not match the agreed parity, an error has occurred and the byte is re-sent. A single parity bit detects any error in an odd number of bits, but it cannot detect two bits being flipped in the same byte, and it cannot show which bit is wrong.
bullets: Parity only detects errors; it does not correct them, so retransmission is requested.
An even number of flipped bits in one byte keeps the parity correct, so the error goes undetected.
The parity bit is usually the most significant bit of the byte.

examples.label: Setting and checking a parity bit
examples.content:
Data bits: 1001101 → four 1s
Even parity: parity bit 0 → 0 1001101
Odd parity: parity bit 1 → 1 1001101
Even parity byte received as 0 1011101: five 1s, which is odd → an error is detected and the byte is re-sent

sections.title: Parity block checks
content: A parity block check extends parity to a block of bytes. Each byte gets its own parity bit (row parity) and, after the block, an extra parity byte is sent in which each bit is the parity of that bit position across all the bytes (column parity). If one bit is flipped, one row and one column will both fail their parity check, and the wrong bit is at the point where they cross. The receiver can therefore correct the error by flipping that bit, without needing a retransmission.
bullets: Row parity finds which byte is wrong; column parity finds which bit position is wrong.
It can locate and correct a single-bit error in the block.
Some combinations of several errors can still cancel out and go undetected.

examples.label: Locating an error with even parity
examples.content:
Bit positions:  P 6 5 4 3 2 1 0
Byte 1:         0 1 0 1 1 0 0 1
Byte 2:         1 0 1 1 0 1 1 1
Byte 3:         1 1 1 1 0 0 1 0   ← five 1s: row parity fails
Byte 4:         1 0 0 0 1 0 1 1
Parity byte:    1 0 0 0 0 1 1 1
Column 4 contains 1, 1, 1, 0 with parity-byte bit 0 → three 1s: column parity fails
The error is in byte 3, bit 4. It was sent as 0 (byte 3 was 1 1100010), so flipping it back corrects the data.

sections.title: Checksums
content: With a checksum, the sender treats each byte in a block of data as a binary number and adds them all together; the result (or a value derived from it, for example the remainder after division) is sent with the block. The receiver performs the same calculation on the data it receives and compares its result with the transmitted checksum. If they differ, an error has occurred and the block is sent again. Like a single parity bit, a checksum detects errors but does not show where they are.
bullets: A checksum checks a whole block, so it can detect errors that single-byte parity misses, such as two flipped bits in one byte.
If the total is too large for the checksum's size, the overflow is discarded or the remainder after division is used.
Checksums are used in network packets and file downloads.

examples.label: Checksum for a block of three bytes
examples.content:
Bytes: 01000001 (65), 00110010 (50), 01111000 (120)
Checksum = 65 + 50 + 120 = 235 → sent with the block
Received bytes add to 65 + 50 + 122 = 237
237 ≠ 235 → error detected, block re-sent

formulas.label: Modulo-11 check digit
formulas.expression: check digit = 11 − (Σ digit × weight mod 11); a result of 11 → 0, 10 → X

formulas.label: Even parity
formulas.expression: parity bit set so that the total number of 1s in the byte is even

formulas.label: Checksum
formulas.expression: checksum = sum of the bytes in the block (overflow discarded)

comparisonTable.title: Methods that protect data integrity
rows: Range, limit, format, length, presence, type, existence checks
Relies on the person noticing errors
Slow; the same error may be made twice
Misses an even number of flipped bits; cannot locate errors
Extra data sent; some multiple errors missed

diagram.title: Parity check on transfer
nodes: Sender and receiver agree odd or even parity
Sender sets the parity bit for each byte
Receiver counts the 1s in each byte

analysisChains.title: Adding validation to an online order form
steps: Presence, format and range checks reject blank, badly formatted or impossible entries
Fewer errors reach the database, so orders are processed correctly
Customers get instant feedback and can correct mistakes
But a customer can still type a valid but wrong address, which validation cannot detect
analysisChains.evaluation: Validation greatly reduces errors but should be combined with verification, such as asking the customer to confirm the order summary.

analysisChains.title: Using a parity block check instead of single-byte parity
steps: Each byte and each bit position across the block has a parity bit
A single flipped bit fails one row check and one column check
The receiver can locate and correct the bit itself
No retransmission is needed, saving time on slow or long-distance links
analysisChains.evaluation: The extra parity byte adds a little data, but correcting errors without retransmission is valuable where resending is slow or impossible.

analysisChains.title: Using double entry for bank account numbers
steps: The account number is typed twice
The system compares the two entries
A typing mistake in either entry means they do not match and the number is rejected
This prevents money being sent to the wrong account
analysisChains.evaluation: Double entry slows data entry, but for high-value data such as payments or new passwords the extra accuracy is worth it.

examTips: State clearly that validation checks data are reasonable, not correct; this is a frequent mark point.
When asked to name a validation check for a field, give the check and an example rule for that field (e.g. 'range check: 0–100').
For parity questions, count the 1s carefully and say whether the agreed parity is odd or even.
For parity block checks, identify the failing row and column and state the bit at their intersection.
Match verification methods to their stage: visual check and double entry for entry; parity and checksum for transfer.
commonMistakes: Saying validation ensures data are correct or accurate.
Mixing up range check (two boundaries) and limit check (one boundary).
Confusing a check digit (part of a stored code) with a checksum (sent with transmitted data).
Claiming a single parity bit can detect every error; two flipped bits in a byte are missed.
Saying a byte parity check can show which bit is wrong.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between validation and verification?
quickRecall.answer: Validation checks data are reasonable and follow rules; verification checks data match the original after entry or transfer.

quickRecall.question: What is an existence check?
quickRecall.answer: A check that the value entered refers to something that exists, such as a customer ID in the customer file.

quickRecall.question: Give two errors a check digit can detect.
quickRecall.answer: Any two of: an incorrect digit, two digits transposed, a missing or extra digit.

quickRecall.question: Name two methods of verification during data entry.
Set the even parity bit for 0110100.
quickRecall.answer: The data contain three 1s, so the parity bit is 1: 1 0110100.

quickRecall.question: What is a limitation of a single parity bit?
quickRecall.answer: It cannot detect an even number of flipped bits in a byte and cannot identify which bit is wrong.

quickRecall.question: How does a parity block check locate an error?
quickRecall.answer: The error is at the intersection of the byte (row) and bit position (column) whose parity checks fail.

quickRecall.question: How does a checksum detect an error?
quickRecall.answer: The receiver recalculates the sum of the received block and compares it with the checksum sent; a difference means an error.
